steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on Vit-lens, which encodes new modalities through a frozen pretrained ViT for omni-modal representation learning, evaluated on 3D shapes. Cover the background and limits of current approaches, our perspective and method, its advantages, and the main 3D results including plugging the encoder into an MLLM.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Omni-modal representation learning; uni-modal foundation models and CLIP; CLIP's limits
- Recent omni-modal models and their reliance on large-scale aligned data
- Our perspective: a pretrained ViT as a multi-modal processor
- Vit-lens method
- Advantages: unification, data efficiency, emergent ability
- 3D evaluation: zero-shot classification results
- Plugging into InstructBlip; closing remarks and future work

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - omni-modal representation learning: focal point, relevant to real-world applications like Embodied AI
  - uni-modal: Transformers + large-scale web data -> general-purpose foundation models for NLP and CV
  - cross-modal: CLIP, milestone, large-scale image-text pairs for pretraining
  - CLIP-based models limited for other sensory modalities: audio, depth, 3D shape
- Omni-modal models
  - ImageBind, ONE-PEACE: one representation model for many modalities
  - modality-specific encoders or modality-shared architecture
  - rely on large-scale cross-modally aligned data (paired with image or text) -> hinders extension to many modalities
  - large-scale data hard to gather for some modalities -> sub-optimal models, poor generalization on novel categories
- Our perspective
  - pretrained ViTs: exceptional generalization and transfer learning
  - adapt their knowledge to novel modalities, no large-scale data / training from scratch per modality (time, resources)
  - conjecture: pretrained ViT as multi-modal processor, senses modalities as it interprets images
- Vit-lens
  - encodes out-of-image modalities through a pretrained ViT, maximize use of pretrained weights
  - modality embedding module + perceiver map input into ViT input space (Figure 1)
  - frozen pretrained ViT encodes further
  - align features with anchor data (images, text, or image-text) via off-the-shelf foundation model
- Advantages
  - (1) Model Unification: shared ViT across modalities, scalable extension, big convergence trend
  - (2) Data-Efficient: no large-scale data needed
  - (3) Emergent Ability: MLLMs rely on vision models to let LLMs see; binding a modality to the ViT of an off-the-shelf MLLM lets the LLM understand it, no instruction tuning
- 3D evaluation
  - follow pre-training paradigms of prior works; joint space of 2D images, text, 3D shapes by binding point clouds to pretrained ViT
  - zero-shot 3D classification, same pretraining data: beats ULIP by 10.2%, ULIP2 by 10.4%, OpenShape by 3.2% on ModelNet40
  - long-tail: Objaverse-LVIS, 1,156 categories, 52.0% zero-shot accuracy, +5.2% over previous SOTA
- InstructBlip and outlook
  - bind 3D to ViT used in InstructBlip (MLLM for 2D images); plug in 3D encoder after pretraining
  - MLLM gains 3D captioning and question answering without instruction tuning
  - simple yet effective; no large-scale data; single set of parameters
  - initial exploration: LLMs sense out-of-image modalities zero-shot
  - future: scale up training, more modalities, more emergent abilities

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Omni-modal representation learning has become a focal point of research, and there is a surge of interest in it because it is relevant to real-world applications like Embodied AI. In the uni-modal setting, the community has used the versatility of Transformers together with lots of large-scale web data, and this gave notable successes in building general-purpose foundation models for Natural Language Processing and Computer Vision. In cross-modal research, the vision-language model CLIP is a significant milestone, which uses large-scale image-text paired data for pretraining. But although it integrates vision and language well, the current CLIP-based models are limited when it comes to other sensory modalities, such as audio, depth, and 3D shape.

Some recent works, for example ImageBind and ONE-PEACE, have started to build a representation model that can cover a wide range of modalities. They use either modality-specific encoders or a modality-shared architecture, and they rely heavily on large-scale data with cross-modal aligned semantics (e.g., paired with image or text). This inevitably makes it hard for them to accommodate a large variety of modalities. In particular, gathering large-scale data for some modalities is not trivial. This gives sub-optimal models that generalize poorly to novel categories, so their wider use in the real world is limited.

In this work we take a different perspective. Pretrained-ViT models have exceptional generalization and transfer learning capabilities, so it is promising to adapt their knowledge to understand novel modalities, instead of collecting large-scale data and training a model from scratch for each modality, which takes a lot of time and resources. Since a pretrained-ViT encodes rich knowledge, we conjecture that it can work as a multi-modal processor – it can sense and understand a spectrum of modalities in the same way as it interprets images.

From this point of view, we introduce Vit-lens, which encodes out-of-image modalities through a pretrained-ViT, with the goal of using the pretrained model weights and the knowledge in them as much as possible. As shown in Figure 1, Vit-lens has a modality embedding module and a perceiver that map the input data into the input space of the pretrained-ViT. Then a frozen pretrained-ViT is used to encode it further. This way diverse modalities can be encoded and their features aligned with the features of anchor data, which can be images, text, or image-text, through an off-the-shelf foundation model.

- Advantages
  - (1) Model Unification: shared ViT across modalities, scalable extension, big convergence trend
  - (2) Data-Efficient: no large-scale data needed
  - (3) Emergent Ability: MLLMs need vision models for LLMs to see; bind modality to ViT of off-the-shelf MLLM -> LLM understands it, no instruction tuning
- 3D evaluation
  - follow prior pre-training paradigms; joint space of 2D images, text, 3D shapes
  - zero-shot, same data: +10.2% over ULIP, +10.4% over ULIP2, +3.2% over OpenShape on ModelNet40
  - Objaverse-LVIS, 1,156 categories: 52.0%, +5.2% over previous SOTA
- InstructBlip and outlook
  - plug 3D encoder into InstructBlip -> 3D captioning and QA, no instruction tuning
  - simple yet effective; single set of parameters; zero-shot out-of-image modalities for LLMs
  - future: scale up, more modalities, more emergent abilities

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Omni-modal representation learning has become a focal point of research, and there is a surge of interest in it because it is relevant to real-world applications like Embodied AI. In the uni-modal setting, the community has used the versatility of Transformers together with lots of large-scale web data, and this gave notable successes in building general-purpose foundation models for Natural Language Processing and Computer Vision. In cross-modal research, the vision-language model CLIP is a significant milestone, which uses large-scale image-text paired data for pretraining. But although it integrates vision and language well, the current CLIP-based models are limited when it comes to other sensory modalities, such as audio, depth, and 3D shape.

Some recent works, for example ImageBind and ONE-PEACE, have started to build a representation model that can cover a wide range of modalities. They use either modality-specific encoders or a modality-shared architecture, and they rely heavily on large-scale data with cross-modal aligned semantics (e.g., paired with image or text). This inevitably makes it hard for them to accommodate a large variety of modalities. In particular, gathering large-scale data for some modalities is not trivial. This gives sub-optimal models that generalize poorly to novel categories, so their wider use in the real world is limited.

In this work we take a different perspective. Pretrained-ViT models have exceptional generalization and transfer learning capabilities, so it is promising to adapt their knowledge to understand novel modalities, instead of collecting large-scale data and training a model from scratch for each modality, which takes a lot of time and resources. Since a pretrained-ViT encodes rich knowledge, we conjecture that it can work as a multi-modal processor – it can sense and understand a spectrum of modalities in the same way as it interprets images.

From this point of view, we introduce Vit-lens, which encodes out-of-image modalities through a pretrained-ViT, with the goal of using the pretrained model weights and the knowledge in them as much as possible. As shown in Figure 1, Vit-lens has a modality embedding module and a perceiver that map the input data into the input space of the pretrained-ViT. Then a frozen pretrained-ViT is used to encode it further. This way diverse modalities can be encoded and their features aligned with the features of anchor data, which can be images, text, or image-text, through an off-the-shelf foundation model.

Our method has several advantages for omni-modal representation learning. (1) Model Unification. Vit-lens uses a shared pretrained-ViT for different modalities, which makes it scalable to extend to new modalities and fits the growing trend of big convergence in multi-modal understanding. (2) Data-Efficient Approach. Vit-lens uses the advanced ViT model effectively, so it is versatile and applicable across diverse tasks and domains without needing large-scale data. (3) Emergent Ability. Recent studies on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown that vision representation models play an essential role in letting Large Language Models (LLMs) perceive and understand the visual world. Interestingly, we find that if we bind a new modality to the ViT used in an off-the-shelf MLLM, the corresponding LLM can sense and understand that modality without any specific instruction tuning.

To show that Vit-lens is effective, we evaluate it on 3D shape understanding. We follow the pre-training paradigms of prior works, but we aim to build a more general and scalable joint representation space for 2D images, text and 3D shapes by binding 3D point clouds to a pretrained-ViT. On zero-shot 3D shape classification, Vit-lens improves a lot over the previous zero-shot state-of-the-art methods. With the same pretraining datasets, Vit-lens beats ULIP by 10.2%, ULIP2 by 10.4%, and OpenShape by 3.2% in zero-shot accuracy on ModelNet40. Vit-lens is also good at long-tail categories. On the challenging Objaverse-LVIS dataset, which has 1,156 categories, Vit-lens gets 52.0% zero-shot accuracy, which is 5.2% better than the previous SOTA.

Besides zero-shot classification, we also bind 3D shapes to the ViT architecture used in InstructBlip, which is an MLLM that can understand and interact over 2D images. After pretraining, we plug the 3D encoder from Vit-lens into InstructBlip to see whether Vit-lens can give the LLM the ability to perceive and understand the 3D modality. This shows that the new variant of the MLLM can do 3D shape captioning and question answering, without specific instruction tuning.

Vit-lens tries to pursue omni-modal representation learning in a simple but effective way, without needing large-scale data collection and with a single set of knowledge expert parameters. Our initial exploration tries to let Large Language Models (LLMs) sense and understand out-of-image modalities in a zero-shot way. Future work can scale up training further to extend Vit-lens to more modalities and look for more emergent abilities.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Omni-modal representation learning has emerged as a focal point of research, attracting a surge of interest owing to its relevance in real-world applications like Embodied AI. In the uni-modal realm, the community has harnessed the versatility of Transformers [5] together with the abundance of large-scale web data, yielding notable successes in developing general-purpose foundation models for Natural Language Processing [6,7,8,9,10,11] and Computer Vision [12,13,14,15,16,17]. In cross-modal research, the vision-language model CLIP [18] is a significant milestone, capitalizing on large-scale image-text paired data for pretraining. While proficient at integrating vision and language, present CLIP-based models are limited in their ability to encompass and interpret additional sensory modalities, such as audio, depth, and 3D shape.

Several recent works, e.g., ImageBind [19] and ONE-PEACE [20], have begun to construct a representation model that can encompass a wide range of modalities. Whether using modality-specific encoders or a modality-shared architecture, they rely heavily on large-scale data with cross-modal aligned semantics (e.g., paired with image or text), which inevitably hinders their ability to accommodate an extensive variety of modalities. Specifically, gathering large-scale data for certain modalities can be non-trivial. This leads to sub-optimal models that generalize poorly to novel categories, hindering their wider application in the real world.

In this work, we present a novel perspective. Given the exceptional generalization and transfer learning capabilities of pretrained-ViT models [18,16,17,21,22], it is promising to adapt their inherent knowledge to comprehend novel modalities, without collecting large-scale data to train models from scratch for each modality, which demands substantial time and resources. Recognizing the rich knowledge encoded in a pretrained-ViT, we conjecture that it can function as a multi-modal processor – it has the capacity to sense and comprehend a spectrum of modalities as it interprets images.

From this standpoint, we introduce Vit-lens, which encodes out-of-image modalities through a pretrained-ViT, aiming to maximize the use of pretrained model weights and the knowledge they encapsulate. As illustrated in Figure 1, Vit-lens integrates a modality embedding module and a perceiver [1] to map input data into the pretrained-ViT input space. A frozen pretrained-ViT is then applied for further encoding. This enables diverse modalities to be encoded, with their features aligned to the established features of anchor data, be it images, text, or image-text, through an off-the-shelf foundation model.

Our method offers several advantages for advancing omni-modal representation learning: (1) Model Unification. Vit-lens adopts a shared pretrained-ViT for various modalities, enabling scalable modality extension in line with the growing trend of big convergence in multi-modal understanding [23]. (2) Data-Efficient Approach. By effectively utilizing the advanced ViT model, Vit-lens achieves versatility and applicability across diverse tasks and domains without the need for large-scale data. (3) Emergent Ability. Recent studies on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) [24,25,26,27,28,29] have underscored the essential role of vision representation models in enabling Large Language Models (LLMs) to perceive and understand the visual world. Interestingly, we find that by binding a new modality to the ViT used in an off-the-shelf MLLM, the corresponding LLM can seamlessly sense and comprehend that modality without any specific instruction tuning.

To demonstrate the effectiveness of Vit-lens, we evaluate it on 3D shape understanding. We follow the pre-training paradigms of prior works [2,3,4], but aim to establish a more generalized and scalable joint representation space covering 2D images, text and 3D shapes by binding 3D point clouds to a pretrained-ViT. On zero-shot 3D shape classification, Vit-lens shows substantial improvements over previous zero-shot state-of-the-art methods. Notably, using the same pretraining datasets, Vit-lens outperforms ULIP [2] by 10.2%, ULIP2 [3] by 10.4%, and OpenShape [4] by 3.2% in zero-shot accuracy on ModelNet40 [30]. Vit-lens also excels on long-tail categories: on the challenging Objaverse-LVIS dataset [31] with 1,156 categories, it achieves 52.0% zero-shot accuracy, surpassing the previous SOTA by 5.2%.

Beyond zero-shot classification, we bind 3D shapes to the ViT architecture used in InstructBlip [29], an MLLM capable of understanding and interacting over 2D images. After pretraining, we plug the 3D encoder produced by Vit-lens into InstructBlip to investigate whether Vit-lens can give the LLM the ability to perceive and comprehend the 3D modality. This integration shows that the new MLLM variant is capable of 3D shape captioning and question answering, without requiring specific instruction tuning.

Vit-lens pursues omni-modal representation learning in a simple yet effective manner, alleviating the need for large-scale data collection and using a single set of knowledge expert parameters. Our initial exploration aims to enable Large Language Models (LLMs) to sense and comprehend out-of-image modalities in a zero-shot manner. Future work can further scale up training to extend Vit-lens to more modalities and explore additional emergent abilities.
